text:
These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day. And even better than simply suppressing it, I agree with Esther Perel, who writes that this sexual energy felt outside the relationship can be used and redirected into the relationship to make it more alive.

Imagine if you and your partner both saw those outside attractions as beneficial energy sources rather than a threat to your relationship. It sure would beat beating around the bush because of fear and jealousy. You can start playing around with opening up about the minor, momentary attractions, rather than wait in hiding until a serious crush is dramatically confessed.

Lots of couples promise forever to each other and nobody else. Look around at how many actually live that way. On the other hand, in a polyamorous relationship, the boundaries might be more negotiable, but then somebody has to sit down and negotiate them, down to who gets to stay the night. That can end up sometimes creating more drama than it's worth.

Polyamory can also be a way of escaping deeper intimacy, like my one poly college friend who boasted about having 4 girlfriends, but admitted to me that he felt deeply unhappy. Or it can be a way of escaping guilt, like when someone keeps cheating until they finally "come out of the closet" as poly, as if that solves their prior dishonesty. But they are right to finally come clean and hopefully avoid that dishonesty in future.

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I'm still not sure about all of it.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)

question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
